Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "Mara Venn booked the back room at Northline Music for a Thursday drum rehearsal, choosing the 6:30–9:00 p.m. slot because the band’s bassist worked until six and the room was close to the bus route he used. The booking was for four people, one drum kit, and a small keyboard amp. Mara entered the band name, Soft Relay, in the studio’s calendar, then added a note asking whether the house kit included a second crash cymbal. She had rehearsed at Northline once before, but that session had been in the smaller room, where the kit was an older three-piece set.

The group was preparing for a short set at the community arts hall the following month. They had not yet settled the order of the songs, and the Thursday rehearsal was meant to give them time to test two possible openings. Mara’s first choice was “Glass Orchard,” a quiet song with a long drum break near the end; the guitarist preferred “Static Map,” which began with a fast count-in. They planned to bring both arrangements and decide after hearing them in the room. The booking itself did not depend on that decision, since either song could be rehearsed with the same setup.

When the confirmation arrived, the room listing showed a standard kit with one crash cymbal, one ride, and a pair of overhead microphones. Mara checked the details against the note she had entered and called the studio in the afternoon. Eli, the evening coordinator, answered and explained that the second crash was usually stored in the teaching room. He could not promise that it would be free on Thursday, because a drum lesson was scheduled there shortly before the band’s slot. Mara said they could bring a cymbal of their own if necessary, but asked him to leave a message in the booking record so the question would not be overlooked.

Eli added the note while they were on the phone. He also confirmed that the room had a bass cabinet and a keyboard stand, although Soft Relay would need to bring its own keyboard amp. Mara corrected the equipment list: the band’s keyboard player had requested the stand, not an amp, and the amp belonged to the guitarist. Eli changed the entry and read the revised note back to her. That small correction mattered because the band shared equipment between rehearsals, and the guitarist was planning to collect his amp from a friend on the way over.

1. The booking record listed the following arrangements:
   - Thursday, 6:30–9:00 p.m., back room
   - Four musicians, including one drummer
   - House kit, bass cabinet, keyboard stand, and two overhead microphones
   - Second crash cymbal requested but not guaranteed

Mara sent the details to the group chat rather than forwarding the studio confirmation. She included the room address, the door code, and the reminder that the side entrance was easier to reach from the bus stop. The guitarist, Leon, replied that he could carry the amp but would arrive close to 6:30. The bassist, Priya, asked whether the band could leave instrument cases along the wall without blocking the fire exit. Mara checked the room diagram attached to the booking page and told her there was a marked storage strip beside the coat hooks.

The next afternoon, the keyboard player, Tom, noticed that the booking page still showed the old equipment note in the confirmation email. Mara compared it with the live calendar, where Eli’s correction appeared under the room details. She called the studio again, not to change the booking, but to make sure the email discrepancy would not lead staff to expect an amp from the band. Eli checked the record and said the calendar was current. He offered to send an updated confirmation, but Mara said it was enough to have the corrected equipment list visible to whoever opened the room that evening.

On Thursday, the band arrived in stages. Priya got there first and put her bass case in the marked strip, leaving the exit clear. Mara reached the desk shortly after six and asked whether the teaching room’s crash cymbal had been returned to storage. The attendant checked the equipment board and said it was still in use for a lesson. He could not say when the lesson would end, so Mara left her own small crash in its bag near the kit. Leon arrived at 6:34 with the amp, and Tom came a few minutes later carrying a compact keyboard and a folding stand of his own.

The house kit was in good condition, though the drummer’s stool needed a slight adjustment. Mara tightened its height collar before the others began unpacking. They spent the first half hour checking the microphones and setting levels, then ran “Glass Orchard” twice. The longer drum break exposed a loose tom mount, which the drummer tightened between takes. They moved on to “Static Map” after a short water break, keeping the count-in at a moderate pace so the keyboard could enter cleanly. No one asked to extend the booking, and the band stopped playing a few minutes before nine to pack the shared room without rushing.

Before leaving, Mara returned the house cymbals to their stands and checked the floor for sticks and cable ties. She made a brief note in the band’s rehearsal log that the room’s bass cabinet had a scratchy input when its cable was moved, while the microphones and keyboard stand had worked as expected. The studio had not charged them for the second crash, since they had used the one they brought. Priya took the booking receipt, and Mara saved the updated equipment list in the group chat for the next rehearsal, which was pencilled in for a different evening at the same venue.", "output": "Mara Venn booked the back room at Northline Music for a Thursday drum rehearsal, choosing the 6:30–9:00 p.m. slot because the band’s bassist worked until six and the room was close to the bus route he used.
